channel.title: Today in Signal history · Signal & Cyber Corps Museum Society
channel.description: A story a day from the history of the U.S. Army Signal Corps and Cyber Corps, from the Signal & Cyber Corps Museum Society's virtual museum.

item.title: November 29, 2016: Breaking Ground for Army Cyber's Headquarters
item.description: On November 29, 2016, Secretary of the Army Eric Fanning and Lt. Gen. Paul Nakasone broke ground at Fort Gordon for the new Army Cyber Command headquarters. The building, later named Fortitude Hall, was dedicated in September 2020. #SignalCorps #ArmyHistory

item.title: November 29, 1911: Army Fliers Winter in Augusta
item.description: On November 29, 1911, the Signal Corps aviation school from College Park, Maryland, arrived in Augusta, Georgia, to keep flying through the winter on the Barnes farm. That winter proved unusually harsh: heavy snow fell in January and February 1912. Pilots trained here included Henry H. "Hap" Arnold and Thomas DeW. Milling. The Signal Corps returned to the Augusta area in 1948 at Camp Gordon. #SignalCorps #ArmyHistory

item.title: November 23, 1977: Veterans at Last
item.description: On November 23, 1977, President Jimmy Carter signed the G.I. Bill Improvement Act. It let the Defense Department recognize certain civilian groups' wartime service as active military service, which opened the way for the Signal Corps' World War I telephone operators to be recognized as veterans. Few of them were still alive. #SignalCorps #ArmyHistory

item.title: On this day in 1877: Telegraph at the Wreck of the Huron
item.description: Early on November 24, 1877, the steamer Huron ran aground off Nags Head, North Carolina. Sgt. S. W. Naylor, the Signal Corps observer at Kitty Hawk, eight miles away, hurried to the scene and set up a telegraph station on the shore. It sent more than 550 messages through December 11. Only 34 of the 132 men aboard survived. #SignalCorps #ArmyHistory
